title: WHY JESUS TOLD A MAN TO “LET THE DEAD BURY THEIR DEAD”
paragraphs:
WHY JESUS TOLD A MAN TO “LET THE DEAD BURY THEIR DEAD”
One of Jesus’ Harshest-Sounding Commands Wasn’t About Disrespecting the Dead—It Was About the Terrifying Danger of Saying “Jesus, But First…”
There are words of Jesus that comfort you immediately.
“Come to Me.”
“Do not be afraid.”
“Your sins are forgiven.”
And then there are words that stop you cold.
Words you read twice because they almost do not sound like the Jesus you thought you knew.
A man tells Jesus that he wants to follow Him, but asks permission to do something seemingly honorable first.
Bury his father.
And Jesus answers:
“Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God.” — Luke 9:60, KJV
At first, it sounds almost cruel.
Was Jesus telling a grieving son to abandon his dead father?
Was He condemning funerals?
Was He teaching Christians to neglect their families?
No.
But what Jesus was saying may be even more uncomfortable than those interpretations.
Because hidden inside this encounter is a warning about one of the most dangerous words you can ever place between yourself and Jesus.
Not “never.”
Not “no.”
Just...
“first.”
And before you finish reading this, you may realize that the unnamed man standing beside Jesus two thousand years ago sounds disturbingly familiar.
Because some of us have never actually told Jesus no.
We have simply spent years telling Him...
“Not yet.”
Luke places the encounter in a section filled with the cost and urgency of discipleship. Jesus is traveling toward Jerusalem. Along the road, people encounter Him and speak about following Him.
One man confidently declares that he will follow Jesus wherever He goes.
Jesus warns him that following the Son of Man offers no guarantee of earthly comfort.
Then Jesus turns to another man.
This time, the man does not initiate the conversation.
Jesus does.
Two words fall upon his life:
“Follow me.” — Luke 9:59, KJV
Imagine hearing that personally.
Not from a preacher.
Not from a devotional.
Not through a screen.
Jesus Christ looks at you and says:
Follow Me.
And the man responds:
“Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father.”
There it is.
“Lord... first.”
Those words belong together far less comfortably than we imagine.
The Greek text makes the tension painfully clear:
Κύριε, ἐπίτρεψόν μοι ἀπελθόντι πρῶτον θάψαι τὸν πατέρα μου.
Kyrie, epitrepson moi apelthonti prōton thapsai ton patera mou.
A straightforward rendering is:
“Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.”
Then comes Jesus’ shocking response:
Ἄφες τοὺς νεκροὺς θάψαι τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς· σὺ δὲ ἀπελθὼν διάγγελλε τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ.
Aphes tous nekrous thapsai tous heautōn nekrous; sy de apelthōn diangelle tēn basileian tou theou.
“Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.”
The word repeated is νεκρός — nekros — “dead.”
Jesus deliberately uses “dead” in two senses.
The physically dead obviously cannot conduct funerals.

So the force of the saying is commonly understood as a contrast between those who are physically alive yet outside the urgent call of discipleship, and those who have been summoned to proclaim God’s kingdom.
Jesus is not confused about death.
He is exposing another kind of death.
A person can breathe...
work...
eat...
laugh...
build a career...
raise children...
scroll through a phone...
sit in church...
sing worship songs...
and still be spiritually dead apart from the life God gives.
The New Testament repeatedly develops that reality.
Paul later writes of people being “dead in trespasses and sins” before God makes them alive with Christ.
Jesus Himself speaks elsewhere of the dead hearing the voice of the Son of God and living.
So when Jesus says, “Let the dead bury their dead,” He is not mocking grief.
He is confronting spiritual priority.
And we should be careful about claiming more than Scripture tells us.

Luke does not explicitly say whether the man's father was lying dead at that moment. Some interpreters have suggested that “bury my father” could mean remaining with his family until his father eventually died. That is possible, and some Bible notes explicitly recognize that the father was not necessarily already dead.
But Scripture does not settle that historical detail for us.
We do not need speculation to feel the force of Jesus' command.
The point Luke gives us is already devastatingly clear:
Jesus called.
The man answered...
“first.”
And perhaps that is where this ancient road suddenly enters your house.
Because what is your “first”?
“Jesus, I will follow You, but first let me get my life together.”
“Jesus, I will surrender this relationship, but first let me see where it goes.”
“Jesus, I know I need to forgive, but first let them apologize.”
“Jesus, I know this habit is destroying me, but first give me one more night.”
“Jesus, I know I should repent, but first let me enjoy myself while I am young.”
“Jesus, I will serve You when life becomes less busy.”
“Jesus, I will open my Bible when I have more time.”
“Jesus, I will tell people about You when I become more confident.”
“Jesus, I will come back to church when I stop feeling ashamed.”
“Jesus, I will surrender everything...
eventually.”
And eventually becomes next month.
Next month becomes next year.
Next year becomes someday.
Someday becomes a lifetime.
Then one day you realize something terrifying:
You never consciously abandoned Jesus.
You just kept postponing Him.
That is why this passage cuts so deeply.
The man's request does not sound wicked.
That matters.
Sin does not always approach wearing the face of obvious rebellion.
Sometimes what competes with obedience is something respectable.
Family.
Career.
Comfort.
Security.
Reputation.
Tradition.
Plans.
Responsibilities.
Things that may be legitimate in themselves can become spiritually destructive when they are placed above the direct claim of Christ.
Jesus is not teaching that parents do not matter.

The same Scriptures command people to honor father and mother. Jesus condemned religious hypocrisy that allowed people to evade legitimate responsibilities toward their parents. At the cross, while suffering unimaginably, Jesus made provision for His mother.
So Luke 9 cannot responsibly be interpreted as Jesus suddenly becoming anti-family.
Something deeper is happening.
Jesus is establishing supremacy.
There is a difference between loving your family...
and allowing family to outrank Christ.
There is a difference between having responsibilities...
and using responsibilities as respectable camouflage for delayed obedience.
There is a difference between saying, “Jesus is important to me”...
and saying, “Jesus is Lord.”
Lordship means Jesus does not simply receive whatever part of your life remains after everything else has taken its share.
He gets the throne.
This becomes even clearer because Luke immediately tells us about another would-be disciple.
Another man says:
“I will follow thee, Lord; but let me first go bid them farewell, which are at home at my house.”
Again.
“I will follow You...”
“But first.”
Jesus responds with another uncompromising image:
“No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.” — Luke 9:62, KJV
Do you see the pattern?
One person wants discipleship without insecurity.
Another wants discipleship after burial.
Another wants discipleship after farewell.
Jesus keeps cutting through every condition placed in front of obedience.
Not because He lacks compassion.
Because He knows something we desperately try to forget:
Delayed surrender can become disguised refusal.
We imagine rebellion always screams:
“I hate God!”
But sometimes rebellion whispers:
“I'll obey tomorrow.”
And tomorrow is one of Satan's most effective counterfeits of repentance.
Because tomorrow feels responsible.
Tomorrow feels possible.
Tomorrow lets your conscience quiet down without requiring your life to change today.
You can cry during worship today and promise surrender tomorrow.
You can feel conviction today and repent tomorrow.
You can know the relationship is sinful today and leave tomorrow.
You can know you need Christ today and decide tomorrow.
You can feel the Holy Spirit exposing something today...
and keep it hidden until tomorrow.
But Scripture never promises you tomorrow.
Jesus calls people in the present tense.
“Follow Me.”
Maybe that is why these words bother us.
We prefer a Jesus who advises.
Jesus commands.
We prefer a Jesus who fits into our existing priorities.
Jesus rearranges them.
We prefer Christianity as an improvement to our lives.
Jesus calls us to lose our lives for His sake.
We want Jesus as Savior from hell while quietly resisting Jesus as Lord over Monday morning.
We want forgiveness without surrender.
Grace without repentance.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A crown without a cross.
But that is not the Gospel Jesus preached.
And strangely...
that is good news.
Because the Jesus who demands everything is the Jesus who gave everything.
The One telling this man to follow Him was walking toward Jerusalem.
Toward betrayal.
Toward mocking.
Toward scourging.
Toward nails.
Toward a Roman cross.
Jesus was not standing safely at a distance demanding sacrifice from other people.
He was walking toward His own.
The hands commanding, “Follow Me,” would soon be pierced.
The feet walking toward Jerusalem would soon be nailed to wood.
The voice proclaiming God's kingdom would cry out beneath the weight of suffering.
And the sinless Son of God would give His life for sinners.
Then the grave would receive Him.
And the grave would fail to keep Him.
That changes everything.
Christian discipleship is not surrender to a tyrant demanding your life for his ego.
It is surrender to the Savior who gave His life to rescue yours.
Jesus is worthy of first place because there is no one like Him.
He carried the judgment sinners deserved.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now the risen Christ does not merely offer you improved behavior.
He offers life.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
A new heart.
A new allegiance.
A new identity.
A new future.
Grace does not mean Jesus lowers the cost of discipleship until nothing has to change.
Grace means you could never purchase salvation at all.
Christ purchased redemption.
And the grace that saves us begins transforming us.
That is where scandal becomes grace.
Maybe your scandal is not public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe there was no headline.
No viral exposure.
No public collapse.
Maybe your scandal lives behind a locked phone.
Inside deleted messages.
Inside bitterness nobody can see.
Inside pornography you keep promising to quit.
Inside pride dressed as spirituality.
Inside resentment toward someone you smile at every Sunday.
Inside a relationship you know dishonors Christ.
Inside money that owns you.
Inside secret compromise.
Inside years of saying:
“Jesus...
first let me...”
And perhaps you have assumed that because you delayed so long, Jesus must finally be finished with you.
Look again at the Gospel.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The thief beside Jesus reached the end of a ruined life with nothing left to offer.
Christ's grace reached sinners in places respectable religion would have considered hopeless.
This does not make sin small.
It makes the Savior enormous.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending your scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything by taking guilty sinners, forgiving those who repent and believe, making them His own, and beginning a transformation only grace could produce.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
But you cannot keep gripping the old pages while asking Jesus to write the new ones.
Repentance means turning.
Faith means trusting Christ.
Following means He leads.
And maybe the sentence you need today is not complicated.
Stop negotiating with the One who died for you.
Stop giving Jesus conditions.
Stop treating surrender like an appointment you can reschedule indefinitely.
Stop saying:
“Lord, first...”
Maybe today the prayer becomes:
“Lord, You first.”
You first before my reputation.
You first before my appetite.
You first before my relationship.
You first before my ambition.
You first before my comfort.
You first before the secret thing I am terrified to surrender.
Not because surrender purchases His love.
Because in Christ you have encountered a love worth surrendering everything to.
Be honest.
There is no prize for pretending you are stronger than you are.
The Gospel begins with the collapse of self-salvation and the discovery that Christ is enough.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this, do not immediately assume this article is only for them.
Let God search you first.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ.

But if Gospel Warrior is helping you encounter Scripture, repent more deeply, understand the Gospel, and keep Jesus before people who desperately need Him, then supporting this work can become one practical expression of generosity and participation in spreading biblical truth.
Your support helps this ministry continue putting the message of Jesus in front of people who may never walk into a church but will stop long enough to read something a friend shared.
And that is why sharing matters too.
It can also become a doorway.
Somebody you know may be silently losing a battle you know nothing about.
Somebody may be questioning whether God could forgive them.
Somebody may be one night away from making another destructive decision.
Somebody may have stopped praying.
Somebody may be ashamed to return to church.
Somebody may not know Jesus at all.
You cannot know where a shared Gospel message will travel.
Return to Luke 9:57–62 when your obedience begins accumulating conditions again.
Invite your family.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the person who has become lukewarm.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who keeps asking difficult questions.
Those things cannot be sold.
You are supporting the work while receiving deeper opportunities for Christian nourishment and resources created to keep pointing people toward Jesus.
But never confuse the invitation.
The question beneath this entire article is whether you are following Jesus.
Because eventually every excuse runs out.
Every possession changes hands.
Every career ends.
Every applause fades.
Every body returns to dust unless Christ returns first.
And suddenly the strange words spoken beside an ancient road do not sound so strange anymore.
“Follow Me.”
The man wanted something first.
Jesus wanted the man.
And perhaps right now...
He is putting His finger on your “first.”
That relationship.
That habit.
That grudge.
That fear.
That ambition.
That secret.
That delay.
That carefully protected corner of your life where you have placed a tiny sign saying:
“Everything but this, Lord.”
What happens next is between you and Jesus.
You can close this article.
You can scroll.
You can tell yourself you will think about it later.
You can feel convicted for five minutes and return unchanged to the same life.
Or you can stop.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Surrender.
Come to Christ again with empty hands.
Not:
“Lord, first...”
But:
“Lord...
You first.”
And if you have wandered, come home.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you are ashamed, run toward Christ rather than away from Him.
If you have never trusted Him, do not imagine that cleaning yourself up first will make you worthy.
You cannot rewrite yourself into righteousness.
That is why you need a Savior.
Jesus Christ receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
The cross says your sin is more serious than you wanted to believe.
The cross also says God's grace is greater than you dared to hope.
And the empty tomb declares that death itself does not get the final sentence.
So share this if someone needs to hear it.
And comment something real.
“Jesus, You first.”
“Pray for me.”
“No more hiding.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or tell your testimony.
Because someone reading the comments may need evidence that grace still reaches people in wreckage.
There is still time to stop saying “Jesus, but first”—but do not make the mistake of assuming there will always be another tomorrow in which to say, “Jesus, You first.”
